summary.qualitative: The candidate is structurally clean — all five sections in order, every section-D item carrying an explicit origin label (often with a secondary origin), no stray commentary — and its coverage of the narrative arc (bug-vs-by-design correction, "your call" delegation, gated execution, the post-baseline pivot, exchanges vs turns, cold-read targeting, ground truth from the ledger) is strong. It is materially weaker on numbers and mid-session engineering detail: it drops the 55,155 cache tokens/$0.576 cold-cell anatomy, the 22,585-char ≤400-char rubric sizing and multi-file-bullet rule, the 41% never-distilled figure, ~$0.002/session, the ~10x projection cut, 11 transcripts, 114 files, 2 commits, the git-identity convention, the <a prior project> provenance of the headless recipe, and — notably — the disclosed ~/.claude-home `-r`/`--continue` trade-off and the transcript-parser iteration. Its grounding is mostly solid, but it invents two assistant errors that never happened (an assumption that config editing would fix home trust; a pre-baseline hypothesis that routing was the expensive step) and inverts two user-behavior readings, recasting the "is it installed / what does it do" questions and the "bug" framing as demonstrated expertise where the reference treats them as growth edges. Net: better than the reference on origin labelling discipline and failure-by-failure command detail, weaker on quantitative fidelity and honest characterization of user knowledge gaps.

The recall rationale (Jev cheap, extractor costly, missing a correction costs the memory) is grounded, but tying it to the "live data is sacred" core value is the candidate's own inference, not stated in the transcript.
candidate_claims.reason: The tune-for-recall decision is real; the secondary origin in the 'live data is sacred' value is an added inference over a principle that does exist in the transcript.
